limitations: No dependency advisory scan: cargo-audit, cargo-deny, osv-scanner, semgrep, and trivy are not installed on this host. Third-party crate risk is unreviewed.
PostgreSQL was not exercised; no server was available. Postgres variants of findings 1 and 3 are confirmed by code and schema reading only.
Codebase-memory graph indexing was unavailable; discovery used grep/glob and direct reading rather than call-graph analysis.
audit.public_issue_sanitisation: Issue bodies on the public repo contain no private/ paths, no requirement.md quotes, and no private file contents. The compliance-erosure argument in #20 is made entirely from public evidence: the beliefs table DDL comment at sql/001_core.sql:335-337.

findings.title: Plaintext triple subject/predicate/object survives compliance erasure

locations.note: triples.subject / predicate / object are plain text NOT NULL columns
inserts SPO verbatim
same insert on the Postgres backend
erase purges item_embeddings, index_pending, items_fts, assoc_edges, memtree_nodes; no statement against triples
same omission on Postgres

findings.description: Triple SPO content is stored as plaintext in the triples table even though the identical content is correctly DEK-sealed inside the carrier item's content_ciphertext. The compliance erasure path never references the triples table, so erasing a data subject destroys the DEK (correctly rendering the carrier item unreadable) while the same content remains readable in cleartext with no key.

requirement_conflict.text_summary: Every memory item's content payload including belief proposition text is stored encrypted under a per-data-subject DEK; only bi-temporal structure may remain in plaintext.
Anything that references or paraphrases erased content must be regenerated so no derived projection continues to describe content that is no longer legible.

findings.contrasting_design: The beliefs table at sql/001_core.sql:335-337 documents the intended rule in its DDL comment: proposition content sealed under the subject DEK, only the normalized identity key and structure plaintext. The triples table applies the opposite treatment to the same kind of content.

reachability.entry_point: MCP tool `triple_add` (crates/clio-mcp/src/write_tools.rs:279, calls clio_write::triple::triple_add at :315, which calls store.commit_triple_add at crates/clio-write/src/triple.rs:210)
reachability.notes: subject/predicate/object are free-text arguments supplied by the model or user invoking the tool.

output: [mcp] triple_add over the real MCP handler -> ok=true

findings.impact: Confidentiality: any reader of the database file, a backup, or a snapshot reads every triple in cleartext; the per-subject DEK offers no protection for this content. Compliance: an erasure request is recorded as successful (tombstone written, DEK destroyed, verification probe passes) while the subject's content remains readable, producing a false attestation of erasure in the system's own audit trail.
findings.fix: Seal the SPO under the subject DEK and retain only a normalized identity key in plaintext, matching the beliefs table design and its DDL comment. Alternatively add triples to the purge in both sqlite_erase_purge.rs and postgres_erase.rs. Add a regression test asserting that triple_add followed by erase_subject leaves no readable copy.

findings.title: XChaCha20-Poly1305 nonce derived from wall clock and plaintext length instead of a CSPRNG

locations.note: seal() derives the nonce; see also the acknowledged shortcut comment at :77-78
content_for() calls seal() once per outgoing mutation
--sync-key / CLIO_SYNC_KEY enables the cipher
MCP sync_key argument builds the cipher

findings.description: The nonce is SHA256("<nanos>|<plaintext_len>" || 0x1f || "am-sync-nonce") truncated to 24 characters, with no random input. Reuse of a (key, nonce) pair repeats the ChaCha20 keystream and the Poly1305 one-time key.

output: [seal] nonce values reused = 42793, worst single-nonce reuse = 8
[leak] msg ct#13836 XOR msg ct#43800 == pt#13836 XOR pt#43800 : true
[leak] recovery matches the true plaintext         : true

findings.impact: An observer holding two ciphertexts under a reused nonce learns the XOR of the plaintexts. One known plaintext — including a guess validated against the cleartext content_hash the protocol already sends (client_feed.rs:236-240) — yields full recovery of the other.
accuracy_corrections: The 24-byte nonce is 24 ASCII hex characters, not 24 raw digest bytes; that is 96 bits of hash output, not 192.
The XOR identity holds for the ciphertext body, not the full ciphertext_b64 value, which appends the 16-byte Poly1305 tag.

A single CLI push is sequential (client.rs:93-99). Reuse arises from genuine concurrency: MCP HTTP serves each connection on its own thread (clio-mcp/src/http.rs:99-106), and multiple clients or devices share one sync_key.

Nonce predictability alone is not a vulnerability; nonces are public. The defect is reuse. Poly1305 key reuse enables forgery only with further known or chosen message-tag pairs, which was not demonstrated.
findings.severity_rationale: Medium as measured. Becomes High against a malicious sync peer or on-path observer that holds one known plaintext, since the server stores client ciphertext verbatim.
findings.fix: Draw 24 raw bytes from OsRng per seal, or use a persisted per-key counter. Add a concurrency uniqueness test; crypto_tests.rs:58-65 only checks two sequential seals differ, which passes merely because the clock ticked.

findings.title: Sync server buffers requests without bound before authenticating, and handles connections serially

locations.note: read_request grows buf with no cap on the header block or the declared Content-Length
read_request is called before any auth decision
authorized() is checked only afterwards
serve_loop handles each connection serially in the accept loop, no thread spawn
5s set_read_timeout, a per-read timeout rather than a total deadline; its result is discarded

findings.description: Unlike the MCP transport, which enforces a 10 MiB MAX_BODY (crates/clio-mcp/src/http.rs:37-38), the sync transport's framing loop grows its buffer until it sees the header terminator and Content-Length bytes. Because the read happens before authorization, an unauthenticated client can occupy the server's single accept slot and grow server memory, without presenting a token.

output: [flood] one connection buffered ~11 MiB in 5.117s with no header terminator
[hol]   legitimate request during one stalled connection: HTTP/1.1 200 OK

findings.impact: Pre-authentication denial of service against the sync peer. Availability only; not an authorization bypass.
accuracy_corrections: The 5s timeout is per-read, not a total request deadline; a client sending one byte every few seconds holds the connection indefinitely.
The default bind is loopback, so exposure requires an operator binding to a LAN or 0.0.0.0 with a token.
The ~11 MiB figure is host-speed dependent. The unbounded-growth property is structural; the number is not portable.
findings.severity_rationale: Medium when network-exposed, Low for the documented loopback default.
findings.fix: Cap the header block and declared body length, add a total request deadline, and replace the serial accept loop with a bounded worker pool.

findings.title: MCP HTTP transport spawns one unbounded thread per connection with no read timeout

locations.note: std::thread::spawn per accepted connection, no cap and no pool
handle_conn blocks in read_request; no read timeout is ever set on the stream
MAX_BODY bounds completed data but not an idle connection
non-loopback binds require a token, but the token is not needed to occupy a thread

findings.description: Each accepted connection allocates a thread that blocks on read with no deadline. Threads accumulate without limit, and thread allocation happens before any authentication or origin decision.

output: [idle] 200 idle connections held open, none authenticated
[serve] after 200 idle conns, authorized request -> HTTP/1.1 200 in 3.4ms
[exhaust] connect() started failing after 14727 extra idle connections
[exhaust] authorized request now -> connect failed: Can't assign requested address

findings.impact: Local or container-level denial of service. Not a privilege escalation.
accuracy_corrections: Request bodies are capped at 10 MiB; the missing protection is the count and lifetime of threads, not body size.
A non-loopback bind cannot start without a token, but authentication runs after the thread is already allocated and blocked in read.
A valid-token holder doing this to themselves is self-DoS, not escalation. Realistic adversaries are an untrusted local process or a setup that publishes the loopback port.
findings.severity_rationale: Low for the documented loopback default; Medium if the listener is exposed.
findings.fix: Set read and write deadlines before parsing, and replace one-thread-per-connection with a bounded worker pool or semaphore.

findings.title: Provider API key and memory payload sent over cleartext http:// to any host

locations.note: HttpEndpoint::parse accepts http:// for any host, not only loopback
embed request attaches authorization: Bearer {key}
health probe path attaches the same header
embed.url / rerank.url / extract.url validated as string only; no scheme or host restriction

findings.description: The sidecar/provider transport, documented as plain http for local sidecars, applies no host restriction. An operator who configures a remote http:// provider URL causes the long-lived provider API key and the memory text being embedded or extracted to be transmitted in cleartext, with no warning at configuration time.

output: [parse] accepted remote http:// -> host=api.vendor.example.com port=80 path=/v1/embed
[wire] provider API key appeared in cleartext on the wire: true
[wire] confidential request payload in cleartext           : true

findings.impact: Disclosure of the provider API key and of memory content to any network observer, plus the ability to read and modify the request in transit.
findings.severity_rationale: Requires an operator configuration choice, but the local-sidecar default is silently extended to arbitrary remote hosts with no guard.
findings.fix: Require https:// for any non-loopback host and warn or refuse on http:// to a remote address, matching the loopback-only rule the MCP HTTP bind already enforces at clio-mcp/src/http.rs:90-96.

examined_and_not_reported.hypothesis: Caller-controlled bank argument crosses a bank boundary in MCP tools
examined_and_not_reported.reasoning: resolve_ctx (crates/clio-mcp/src/runtime_context.rs:69-93) lets the caller name any bank, with a single gate on the reserved `shared` bank. Banks are per-agent namespaces within one deployment, not a tenant boundary. The sync server, which is a genuine multi-party boundary, does enforce an allowlist (crates/clio-sync/src/server.rs:230-232).

sql/001_core.sql:465 is a plaintext column and memtree_attach.rs:54 copies the plaintext gist into it; the row was proven to land in cleartext on disk. However upsert_memtree_node has no production caller. The only call sites are test fixtures (memtree_persist_tests.rs, erase_test_support.rs, task_tests.rs). The live MCP runtime keeps the forest in memory (runtime_open.rs). Worth a guard test before anyone wires the primitive up.

crates/clio-store/src/postgres.rs:54 never uses TLS, so a non-loopback Postgres would carry credentials and content in cleartext. The shipped default is 127.0.0.1 (.env.example:16) and the compose service is local.

examined_and_not_reported.hypothesis: Prompt injection through stored gists into compose_context
examined_and_not_reported.reasoning: The retrieval pack is token-budgeted and section-structured but does not mark memory content as untrusted data. This is inherent to any memory system; no concrete injection path was demonstrated.
Erase deletes the leaf and NULLs ancestor summaries (sqlite_erase_purge.rs:113-161), but the ancestor walk caps at 64 hops. Superseded by CLIO-SEC-001, which is the material gap.
